# Hot-air engine (Stirling) (`hot_air_engine`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/energy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Energy & engines (`energy`)
- Deps: needs boring_machine, crank_connecting_rod; helped by gas_laws, heat_energy_conservation
- Core idea: A fixed quantity of air is sealed in a cylinder, one end kept hot by a fire, the other cooled by water. A loose-fitting displacer piston shuttles the air between the hot and the cold end; when most of the air is at the hot end the pressure rises and pushes a second, tight working piston, when it is at the cold end the pressure falls and the piston returns. The two pistons work on cranks a quarter turn apart. On its way the air passes through a mass of wire or thin plates (the regenerator), which stores the heat of the air going to the cold end and gives it back on the return; that is what makes the engine economical. There is no boiler to burst and any fuel will do, but it gives little power for its size.
- Pitfalls:
  - Expecting steam-engine power; working pressures are low unless the air is pressurised
  - The hot end burns out: an iron heater at dull red heat under pressure does not last
  - Leaving out the regenerator, or the quarter-turn phase between the two pistons
  - Leaks; the engine works on a sealed charge of air
- History: europe: 1807 – George Cayley's open-cycle hot-air engine; 1816 Robert Stirling's patent with the regenerator ('economiser'); 1818 first engine pumping water at an Ayrshire quarry; 1843 engine at a Dundee foundry, abandoned when its heaters failed; 1938 revived by Philips; americas: 1833–1858 – John Ericsson's caloric engines; thousands of small pumping engines sold from the 1870s
- Read:
  - Theodor Finkelstein & Allan J. Organ, Air Engines: The History, Science, and Reality of the Perfect Engine (2001)
